doc.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Singing on stage versus in the studio, and going there
summary: She compares stage and studio and describes the acting advice to just go where the lyric takes you.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I’ve heard you referred to, these are some great phrases, “a professor emeritus of body language,” “a consummate actress,” or in your own words, a ham. Is there a way that you approach a song?
I’ve never given it any conscious thought.
Is there a difference for you, singing on stage versus in the studio?
The recording can be very boring. I like to get on the stage and do the thing and just get it, just do it. In the studio it’s a lot different. I rarely ever do more than three takes of a song.

Maybe it depends on what day that question gets asked of you, because I have heard a different response from you on this. I have heard you talk about being able, in the studio, without an audience, to “go there.”
Oh, that’s the same thing as being the actress, the song stylist, the singer. She goes there. That’s on stage and in the studio. Go inside that song and make it happen.
So you don’t have to have an audience to make it happen?
And you never had acting lessons either.

No. I did ask a prominent actor, when I was getting ready to do something for television, a dramatic role, what is there about it? He gave me the words, “Just go there.” I’ve used that. It was [?] who told me that. He said, “Just go there.” So that’s what I do when I sing. There’s no way to prepare to go into an acting role without ever having done it before. So he just said, just go where the lyric, where the – what is the word I’m trying to think of? What were the words that are on the paper? Go where they take you.
